items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A push or pull on an object, measured in newtons (N); a vector quantity"?
items.answer: force
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of force.

items.stem: A student claims that if an object is moving, there must be a resultant force on it. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A resultant force is needed to change motion; an object moving at constant velocity has zero resultant force.
items.markingKey: A resultant force is needed to change motion; an object moving at constant velocity has zero resultant force. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between weight and mass.
items.answer: Mass is the amount of matter (kg), the same everywhere; weight is the gravitational force (N) and changes with g (e.g. smaller on the Moon).
items.markingKey: Mass is the amount of matter (kg), the same everywhere; weight is the gravitational force (N) and changes with g (e.g. smaller on the Moon). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Jonas hung masses on a newton meter on Earth to investigate the relationship between mass and weight.

Mass / kg | Weight / N: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.1 | 0.89 | 0.93 | 0.86
0.2 | 1.78 | 1.76 | 1.79
0.3 | 2.69 | 2.79 | 2.64
0.4 | 3.73 | 3.69 | 3.60
0.5 | 4.60 | 4.39 | 4.43

State the mass at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 0.5 kg; range = 0.21 N; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 0.5 kg; 1 range = max − min = 4.60 − 4.39 = 0.21 N; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Lars wants to find out how the mass of a wooden block affects the force needed to pull it at a steady speed across a bench. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does total mass of the block plus added masses affect pulling force in N?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (total mass of the block plus added masses (kg)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (pulling force in N read from a newton meter while the block moves at steady speed (equals friction)) in a question form.

items.stem: Rafael investigated how the mass of a wooden block affects the force needed to pull it at a steady speed across a bench. The method had this weakness: the block was jerked into motion and the peak reading was recorded. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: read the force once the block is moving at a steady speed (or use a force sensor and take the mean steady reading)
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: read the force once the block is moving at a steady speed (or use a force sensor and take the mean steady reading)

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A diagram of one object showing all the forces acting on it as labelled arrows from the object"?
items.answer: free-body diagram
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of free-body diagram.

items.stem: Distinguish between balanced forces and unbalanced forces.
items.answer: Balanced forces give zero resultant – the object stays at rest or at constant velocity; unbalanced forces give a resultant that changes the speed or direction.
items.markingKey: Balanced forces give zero resultant – the object stays at rest or at constant velocity; unbalanced forces give a resultant that changes the speed or direction. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Two tugboats pull a ship with forces of 800 N east and 1500 N north. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force and its angle north of east.
items.answer: 1700 N at 61.9° north of east

items.stem: "Free-body diagrams are the most useful tool for solving force problems." Discuss.
items.answer: They are very useful for most problems, especially with several forces, though calculations still require vector addition.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: make all forces and directions clear; help find the resultant and apply F = ma; reduce mistakes. Arguments against: difficult for forces at angles or rotating objects; not needed for very simple one-force problems. Supported judgement: They are very useful for most problems, especially with several forces, though calculations still require vector addition. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: If the resultant force on an object doubles and its mass stays the same, what happens to its acceleration?
items.answer: It doubles
items.markingKey: A. a ∝ F.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Newton’s second law and Newton’s first law.
items.answer: The first law says no resultant force means no change in velocity; the second law quantifies what happens when there is a resultant force: F = ma.
items.markingKey: The first law says no resultant force means no change in velocity; the second law quantifies what happens when there is a resultant force: F = ma. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between Newton’s first law and Newton’s second law.
items.answer: The first law says no resultant force means no change in velocity; the second law quantifies what happens when there is a resultant force: F = ma.
items.markingKey: The first law says no resultant force means no change in velocity; the second law quantifies what happens when there is a resultant force: F = ma. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Calculate the resultant force needed to give a 2.5 kg trolley an acceleration of 1.2 m/s².
items.answer: 3 N

items.stem: With reference to crash-test dummies in car safety testing, explain how it illustrates Newton’s first and second laws.
items.answer: Cars are crashed at 64 km/h into barriers; sensors in dummies record the forces on the head and chest. The dummy keeps moving (first law) until a force stops it; airbags and crumple zones lengthen the stopping time, reducing deceleration and so the force (F = ma).
items.markingKey: Context (Cars are crashed at 64 km/h into barriers; sensors in dummies record the forces on the head and chest.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The dummy keeps moving (first law) until a force stops it; airbags and crumple zones lengthen the stopping time, reducing deceleration and so the force (F = ma). – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to Newton’s first and second laws.

items.stem: Tomás writes: "A heavier object always falls faster than a light one." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Without air resistance all objects fall with the same acceleration g, because a larger weight acts on a proportionally larger mass (a = W/m = g).
items.markingKey: Without air resistance all objects fall with the same acceleration g, because a larger weight acts on a proportionally larger mass (a = W/m = g). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Newton’s laws explain all motion we observe.
items.answer: Newton’s laws are excellent for everyday speeds and sizes but are approximations of more general theories.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: accurately predict motion from cars to planets; used to design vehicles, bridges and spacecraft. Arguments against: fail near the speed of light (relativity); do not apply to atoms and electrons (quantum mechanics); GPS satellites need relativistic corrections. Supported judgement: Newton’s laws are excellent for everyday speeds and sizes but are approximations of more general theories.

items.stem: Leila investigated how the resultant force on a trolley affects its acceleration (Newton’s second law). The method had this weakness: masses were added to the hanger from the bench, so the total mass increased. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: transfer masses from the trolley to the hanger so the total accelerated mass stays constant
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: transfer masses from the trolley to the hanger so the total accelerated mass stays constant

items.stem: Explain why a seat belt reduces injury in a crash, using Newton’s first law.
items.answer: When the car stops suddenly, the passenger keeps moving forwards (inertia); the seat belt provides the force to decelerate the passenger with the car, over a longer time and distance, rather than the passenger hitting the dashboard.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When the car stops suddenly, the passenger keeps moving forwards (inertia); the seat belt provides the force to decelerate the passenger with the car, over a longer time and distance, rather than the passenger hitting the dashboard. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that a force is needed to keep an object moving at constant speed. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A resultant force is needed only to change velocity; at constant speed forces are balanced (driving force equals resistance).
items.markingKey: A resultant force is needed only to change velocity; at constant speed forces are balanced (driving force equals resistance). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Lars wants to find out how the resultant force on a trolley affects its acceleration (Newton’s second law). Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does resultant force affect acceleration?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (resultant force – weight of hanging masses on a string over a pulley (0.2 to 1.0 N)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (acceleration – from light gates and a data logger (m/s²)) in a question form.

items.stem: A student claims that a heavier object always falls faster than a light one. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Without air resistance all objects fall with the same acceleration g, because a larger weight acts on a proportionally larger mass (a = W/m = g).
items.markingKey: Without air resistance all objects fall with the same acceleration g, because a larger weight acts on a proportionally larger mass (a = W/m = g). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Newton’s third law"?
options: An object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force
A push or pull on an object, measured in newtons (N); a vector quantity
When two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other
The distance travelled while the brakes are applied until the vehicle stops
items.answer: When two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other
items.markingKey: C. "Newton’s third law" is when two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other.

items.stem: Explain the difference between balanced forces on one object and a Newton’s third law pair.
items.answer: A third-law pair acts on two different objects and are the same type; balanced forces act on the same object and can be different types (e.g. weight and normal force).
items.markingKey: A third-law pair acts on two different objects and are the same type; balanced forces act on the same object and can be different types (e.g. weight and normal force). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why third-law forces never cancel each other.
items.answer: They act on different objects, so each affects the motion of a different object; forces only cancel when they act on the same object.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They act on different objects, so each affects the motion of a different object; forces only cancel when they act on the same object. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Felix (40 kg) and Leila (80 kg) stand on skateboards and push each other apart. Felix pushes Leila with 150 N. State the force on Felix and calculate the acceleration of each.
items.answer: 150 N on Felix (opposite direction); Felix 3.75 m/s², Leila 1.88 m/s²
items.markingKey: 1 150 N, opposite direction (third law); 1 150/40 = 3.75 m/s²; 1 150/80 = 1.88 m/s².

items.stem: Outline one way in which SpaceX Falcon 9 launches shows Newton’s third law.
items.answer: The engines expel hot gases downwards at around 3 km/s, producing over 7 MN of thrust. The rocket pushes gas downwards, so the gas pushes the rocket upwards with an equal force.
items.markingKey: Context (The engines expel hot gases downwards at around 3 km/s, producing over 7 MN of thrust.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The rocket pushes gas downwards, so the gas pushes the rocket upwards with an equal force. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to Newton’s third law.

items.stem: Ingrid plans an investigation into how the volume of water in a bottle rocket affects the height it reaches. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (volume of water in a 2 dm³ bottle (200, 400, 600, 800, 1000 cm³)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "interaction pair"?
options: The force exerted by a surface on an object, acting at right angles to the surface
Two forces of the same type and size acting in opposite directions on two different objects
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined
Shaping an object so that air or water flows smoothly around it, reducing drag
items.answer: Two forces of the same type and size acting in opposite directions on two different objects
items.markingKey: B. "interaction pair" is two forces of the same type and size acting in opposite directions on two different objects.

items.stem: "In a collision between a truck and a small car, the truck exerts a bigger force on the car." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The forces are equal and opposite; the car has a smaller mass so its acceleration (and damage) is greater.
items.markingKey: The forces are equal and opposite; the car has a smaller mass so its acceleration (and damage) is greater. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Maya is investigating how the volume of water in a bottle rocket affects the height it reaches. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: volume of water in a 2 dm³ bottle (200, 400, 600, 800, 1000 cm³)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: volume of water in a 2 dm³ bottle (200, 400, 600, 800, 1000 cm³) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that Newton’s third law means it is impossible to win a tug-of-war?
items.answer: The third law does not prevent winning; the winner pushes harder against the ground.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the rope tension pulls both teams equally. Arguments against: the team that pushes harder on the ground gets a larger forward friction force from the ground; the resultant force on each team depends on ground friction minus rope tension. Supported judgement: The third law does not prevent winning; the winner pushes harder against the ground. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which change increases the air resistance on a cyclist?
items.answer: Sitting upright instead of crouching
items.markingKey: Sitting upright instead of crouching. Larger frontal area increases drag.

items.stem: Distinguish between friction between solid surfaces and air resistance.
items.answer: Solid friction acts between surfaces in contact and is roughly independent of speed; air resistance acts on objects moving through air and increases rapidly with speed.
items.markingKey: Solid friction acts between surfaces in contact and is roughly independent of speed; air resistance acts on objects moving through air and increases rapidly with speed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "When a parachute opens, the skydiver moves upwards." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: She still moves downwards but decelerates, because air resistance briefly exceeds her weight.
items.markingKey: She still moves downwards but decelerates, because air resistance briefly exceeds her weight. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Mohammed dropped cupcake cases from 2.0 m and measured the terminal velocity reached for different numbers of stacked cases (more cases = more weight, same shape).

Number of cases | Terminal velocity / m/s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 0.85 | 0.86 | 0.87
2 | 1.22 | 1.18 | 1.18
3 | 1.48 | 1.56 | 1.48
4 | 1.81 | 1.76 | 1.77
5 | 1.98 | 2.02 | 1.93

Calculate the mean terminal velocity when the number of cases was 3 .
items.markingKey: M1 (1.48 + 1.56 + 1.48) ÷ 3; A1 1.51 m/s (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: In an investigation into how the surface area of a paper parachute affects the time it takes to fall 2.0 m, state the dependent variable and describe how Jonas should measure it.
items.answer: time to fall 2.0 m, measured with a stopwatch or from video
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: time to fall 2.0 m, measured with a stopwatch or from video.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Cyclists should always be required to wear helmets."
items.answer: Helmets clearly protect individuals; whether laws should require them depends on balancing safety with encouraging cycling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: helmets reduce the force on the head by increasing the stopping time and spreading the impact; reduce serious head injuries. Arguments against: compulsory laws may reduce cycling, harming public health; separated cycle lanes reduce crashes more; helmets do not protect against all injuries. Supported judgement: Helmets clearly protect individuals; whether laws should require them depends on balancing safety with encouraging cycling.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Shaping an object so that air or water flows smoothly around it, reducing drag"?
items.answer: streamlining
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of streamlining.

items.stem: A student claims that when a parachute opens, the skydiver moves upwards. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: She still moves downwards but decelerates, because air resistance briefly exceeds her weight.
items.markingKey: She still moves downwards but decelerates, because air resistance briefly exceeds her weight. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Formula 1 car aerodynamics as an example, explain friction and air resistance.
items.answer: Wings and the car floor create downforce, pushing tyres onto the track for more grip, but also add drag. More downforce increases friction between tyres and track for cornering, while drag limits top speed – engineers balance the two.
items.markingKey: Context (Wings and the car floor create downforce, pushing tyres onto the track for more grip, but also add drag.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: More downforce increases friction between tyres and track for cornering, while drag limits top speed – engineers balance the two. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to friction and air resistance.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that cyclists should always be required to wear helmets.
items.answer: Helmets clearly protect individuals; whether laws should require them depends on balancing safety with encouraging cycling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: helmets reduce the force on the head by increasing the stopping time and spreading the impact; reduce serious head injuries. Arguments against: compulsory laws may reduce cycling, harming public health; separated cycle lanes reduce crashes more; helmets do not protect against all injuries. Supported judgement: Helmets clearly protect individuals; whether laws should require them depends on balancing safety with encouraging cycling. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The product of mass and velocity, p = m × v, measured in kg m/s; a vector"?
items.answer: momentum
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of momentum.

items.stem: Explain why using a mobile phone while driving increases stopping distance.
items.answer: Distraction increases reaction time, so the car travels further at full speed before braking begins (larger thinking distance).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Distraction increases reaction time, so the car travels further at full speed before braking begins (larger thinking distance). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Road-safety data used by Isabel show the braking distance of a typical car on a dry road at different speeds (three tests per speed).

Speed / m/s | Braking distance / m: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
9 | 6.3 | 6.1 | 6.2
13 | 13.3 | 13.0 | 12.5
18 | 23.9 | 25.5 | 25.5
22 | 38.3 | 35.6 | 38.3
27 | 55.5 | 57.1 | 55.8

Calculate the mean braking distance when the speed was 9 m/s.
items.markingKey: M1 (6.3 + 6.1 + 6.2) ÷ 3; A1 6.20 m (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: In a crash a 60 kg passenger moving at 15 m/s is brought to rest. Calculate the average force on the passenger if she stops in (a) 0.01 s by hitting the dashboard and (b) 0.1 s with an airbag. Explain the difference.
items.answer: (a) 9e+04 N (b) 9000 N; the airbag increases the stopping time, so the force is smaller
items.markingKey: M1 Δp = 60 × 15 = 900 kg m/s; A1 9e+04 N; A1 9000 N; 1 F = Δp/t, longer t gives smaller F.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Car manufacturers should make vehicles that protect pedestrians as well as passengers."
items.answer: Vehicle design should consider all road users; regulation (e.g. Euro NCAP pedestrian ratings) encourages this.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: softer bonnets, pop-up bonnets and external airbags increase the time of impact for pedestrians, reducing force; pedestrians and cyclists are a large share of road deaths. Arguments against: adds cost and weight; large SUVs with high fronts are popular but more dangerous to pedestrians. Supported judgement: Vehicle design should consider all road users; regulation (e.g. Euro NCAP pedestrian ratings) encourages this.

items.stem: Briefly explain why airbags reduce injuries in a collision.
items.answer: The airbag increases the time over which the passenger’s momentum is reduced to zero; since force = change in momentum ÷ time, the force on the passenger is smaller.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The airbag increases the time over which the passenger’s momentum is reduced to zero; since force = change in momentum ÷ time, the force on the passenger is smaller. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that a heavy truck and a car at the same speed have the same momentum. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Momentum depends on mass: the truck has much more momentum and needs a larger force or longer time to stop.
items.markingKey: Momentum depends on mass: the truck has much more momentum and needs a larger force or longer time to stop. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using ideas about momentum and force, explain how crumple zones, seat belts and airbags work together to reduce injuries in a 50 km/h crash, and suggest why a passenger without a seat belt in the back seat endangers people in the front.
items.answer: In a crash the car and occupants must lose all their momentum; F = Δp ÷ t, so increasing the stopping time reduces force. Crumple zones deform, extending the car’s stopping time; seat belts stretch slightly and hold passengers to the decelerating car; airbags cushion the head over a longer time and larger area. An unbelted rear passenger keeps moving (first law) and hits front occupants with a large force.
items.markingKey: In a crash the car and occupants must lose all their momentum; F = Δp ÷ t, so increasing the stopping time reduces force. Crumple zones deform, extending the car’s stopping time; seat belts stretch slightly and hold passengers to the decelerating car; airbags cushion the head over a longer time and larger area. An unbelted rear passenger keeps moving (first law) and hits front occupants with a large force.

items.stem: Why do passengers lurch forwards when a bus brakes suddenly?
options: Their bodies tend to keep moving at the original velocity (inertia)
items.answer: Their bodies tend to keep moving at the original velocity (inertia)
items.markingKey: D. Newton’s first law.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "resultant force"?
options: The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined
The distance travelled during the driver’s reaction time before the brakes are applied
The force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²
The frictional force on an object moving through air, which increases with speed
items.answer: The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined
items.markingKey: A. "resultant force" is the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "Newton’s third law".
items.answer: When two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: when two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between air resistance and friction between solid surfaces.
items.answer: Solid friction acts between surfaces in contact and is roughly independent of speed; air resistance acts on objects moving through air and increases rapidly with speed.
items.markingKey: Solid friction acts between surfaces in contact and is roughly independent of speed; air resistance acts on objects moving through air and increases rapidly with speed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between kinetic energy and momentum.
items.answer: Momentum is mv (vector, kg m/s) and is always conserved in collisions; kinetic energy is ½mv² (scalar, J) and is often partly transferred to heat and sound.
items.markingKey: Momentum is mv (vector, kg m/s) and is always conserved in collisions; kinetic energy is ½mv² (scalar, J) and is often partly transferred to heat and sound. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why a rocket’s acceleration increases as it burns fuel, even with constant thrust.
items.answer: Its mass decreases as fuel is used; with the same resultant force, a = F/m increases (and weight also falls).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Its mass decreases as fuel is used; with the same resultant force, a = F/m increases (and weight also falls). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Maya writes: "An astronaut has no mass on the Moon." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Mass is unchanged; her weight is about one-sixth of her Earth weight because g on the Moon is 1.6 N/kg.
items.markingKey: Mass is unchanged; her weight is about one-sixth of her Earth weight because g on the Moon is 1.6 N/kg. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a Newton’s third law pair and balanced forces on one object.
items.answer: A third-law pair acts on two different objects and are the same type; balanced forces act on the same object and can be different types (e.g. weight and normal force).
items.markingKey: A third-law pair acts on two different objects and are the same type; balanced forces act on the same object and can be different types (e.g. weight and normal force). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why lubricating moving parts of a machine improves efficiency.
items.answer: Oil reduces friction between surfaces, so less energy is wasted as heat and less wear occurs.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Oil reduces friction between surfaces, so less energy is wasted as heat and less wear occurs. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Noah wants to find out how the speed of a trolley affects its stopping distance when it runs onto a rough carpet (modelling braking distance). Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does speed of the trolley when it reaches the carpet affect stopping distance on the carpet?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (speed of the trolley when it reaches the carpet (set by release height on a ramp and measured with a light gate)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (stopping distance on the carpet measured with a metre rule) in a question form.

items.stem: Using David Scott’s hammer and feather drop on the Moon (Apollo 15, 1971) as an example, explain Newton’s second law and free fall.
items.answer: He dropped a 1.32 kg hammer and a 30 g falcon feather together; they hit the ground at the same moment. With no air, the only force is weight; a = W/m = g for both, so they accelerate equally.
items.markingKey: Context (He dropped a 1.32 kg hammer and a 30 g falcon feather together; they hit the ground at the same moment.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: With no air, the only force is weight; a = W/m = g for both, so they accelerate equally. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to Newton’s second law and free fall.

items.stem: Outline one way in which a tug-of-war contest shows resultant forces.
items.answer: When both teams pull with 2000 N the rope does not move; when one team pulls with 2200 N the rope accelerates towards them. Equal and opposite pulls give zero resultant; a 200 N resultant accelerates the rope and teams.
items.markingKey: Context (When both teams pull with 2000 N the rope does not move; when one team pulls with 2200 N the rope accelerates towards them.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Equal and opposite pulls give zero resultant; a 200 N resultant accelerates the rope and teams. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to resultant forces.

items.stem:
Lars launched a 2 dm³ water rocket at 4 bar with different volumes of water and estimated the maximum height using angle measurements.

Volume of water / cm³ | Maximum height / m: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
200 | 23.2 | 23.1 | 22.6
400 | 29.3 | 29.3 | 29.2
600 | 29.5 | 30.1 | 19.3
800 | 27.7 | 26.4 | 26.8
1000 | 18.6 | 18.7 | 18.5

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean maximum height at 600 cm³, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 19.3 m (trial 3 at 600 cm³); mean = 29.80 m
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (19.3) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 29.80 m.

items.stem: A 90 kg skydiver is falling; air resistance on her is 400 N. Calculate her acceleration at that moment (g = 9.8 N/kg).
items.answer: 5.36 m/s² downwards
items.markingKey: M1 W = 882 N; M1 resultant = 882 − 400 = 482 N; A1 a = 5.36 m/s².

items.stem: Using 20 mph (32 km/h) zones in cities such as London and Paris as an example, explain stopping distances.
items.answer: Studies found fewer and less severe casualties after limits were lowered from 30 mph to 20 mph. Lower speed shortens thinking and braking distances, and a pedestrian is hit at a much lower speed, with far less kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: Context (Studies found fewer and less severe casualties after limits were lowered from 30 mph to 20 mph.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Lower speed shortens thinking and braking distances, and a pedestrian is hit at a much lower speed, with far less kinetic energy. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to stopping distances.

items.stem:
Sofia pulled a 1.0 kg trolley with different constant forces and measured its acceleration with light gates.

Resultant force / N | Acceleration / m/s²: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.5 | 0.49 | 0.48 | 0.48
1.0 | 0.93 | 0.94 | 0.98
1.5 | 1.46 | 1.42 | 1.43
2.0 | 1.97 | 1.92 | 1.87
2.5 | 2.40 | 2.37 | 2.43

Calculate the mean acceleration when the resultant force was 1.5 N.
items.markingKey: M1 (1.46 + 1.42 + 1.43) ÷ 3; A1 1.44 m/s² (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that free-body diagrams are the most useful tool for solving force problems.
items.answer: They are very useful for most problems, especially with several forces, though calculations still require vector addition.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: make all forces and directions clear; help find the resultant and apply F = ma; reduce mistakes. Arguments against: difficult for forces at angles or rotating objects; not needed for very simple one-force problems. Supported judgement: They are very useful for most problems, especially with several forces, though calculations still require vector addition.

items.stem: A skater of mass 60 kg pushes a friend of mass 40 kg on ice with a force of 120 N for 0.5 s. (a) State the force on the skater and its direction. (b) Calculate the acceleration of each. (c) Explain why they move apart with different speeds.
items.answer: (a) 120 N in the opposite direction (third law). (b) skater 120/60 = 2 m/s²; friend 120/40 = 3 m/s². (c) Equal forces act for the same time but on different masses, so the lighter friend accelerates more and moves faster (1.5 m/s vs 1.0 m/s).
items.markingKey: (a) 120 N in the opposite direction (third law). (b) skater 120/60 = 2 m/s²; friend 120/40 = 3 m/s². (c) Equal forces act for the same time but on different masses, so the lighter friend accelerates more and moves faster (1.5 m/s vs 1.0 m/s).

items.stem: To what extent is it true that reducing friction is always desirable in engineering?
items.answer: Friction should be reduced where it wastes energy but increased where grip and braking are needed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: less energy wasted, higher efficiency; less wear on parts. Arguments against: friction is essential for brakes, tyres, walking and holding objects; low friction roads are dangerous in rain or ice. Supported judgement: Friction should be reduced where it wastes energy but increased where grip and braking are needed. items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the speed of a trolley affects its stopping distance when it runs onto a rough carpet (modelling braking distance). In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Set ramp at a fixed angle; release trolley from 5 heights; light gate at bottom measures speed; trolley runs onto a 2 m strip of carpet; measure stopping distance; 3 repeats per height; plot stopping distance against speed² to test proportionality.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (keep the run-off area clear and stop the trolley safely at the end). Model: Set ramp at a fixed angle; release trolley from 5 heights; light gate at bottom measures speed; trolley runs onto a 2 m strip of carpet; measure stopping distance; 3 repeats per height; plot stopping distance against speed² to test proportionality.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Newton’s first law"?
options: The distance travelled while the brakes are applied until the vehicle stops
The force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²
The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to its mass: F = ma
An object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force
items.answer: An object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force
items.markingKey: D. "Newton’s first law" is an object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force.

items.stem: What is the unit of force?
items.answer: Newton (N)
items.markingKey: D. 1 N = 1 kg m/s².

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "thrust".
items.answer: The forward force produced when an engine pushes gas or water backwards
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the forward force produced when an engine pushes gas or water backwards. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Aiko writes: "When a parachute opens, the skydiver moves upwards." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: She still moves downwards but decelerates, because air resistance briefly exceeds her weight.
items.markingKey: She still moves downwards but decelerates, because air resistance briefly exceeds her weight. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why stopping distance increases more than in proportion to speed.
items.answer: Thinking distance is proportional to speed, but braking distance is proportional to speed squared (braking work = kinetic energy = ½mv²), so stopping distance rises rapidly at higher speeds.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Thinking distance is proportional to speed, but braking distance is proportional to speed squared (braking work = kinetic energy = ½mv²), so stopping distance rises rapidly at higher speeds. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between inertia and momentum.
items.answer: Inertia is the tendency to resist change in motion, depending on mass; momentum is mass × velocity, a vector that depends on how fast the object moves.
items.markingKey: Inertia is the tendency to resist change in motion, depending on mass; momentum is mass × velocity, a vector that depends on how fast the object moves. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why free-body diagrams only show forces acting on the chosen object.
items.answer: The motion of an object depends only on the forces acting on it; including forces it exerts on other objects would give the wrong resultant.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The motion of an object depends only on the forces acting on it; including forces it exerts on other objects would give the wrong resultant. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the Earth does not noticeably accelerate towards a falling ball, even though the forces are equal.
items.answer: a = F/m; the Earth’s mass is about 6 × 10²⁴ kg, so the same force produces a negligibly small acceleration.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: a = F/m; the Earth’s mass is about 6 × 10²⁴ kg, so the same force produces a negligibly small acceleration. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "At terminal velocity there are no forces acting on the falling object." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Weight and air resistance still act; they are equal and opposite, so the resultant is zero.
items.markingKey: Weight and air resistance still act; they are equal and opposite, so the resultant is zero. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that braking distance doubles when speed doubles. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Braking distance is proportional to v², so it increases four times.
items.markingKey: Braking distance is proportional to v², so it increases four times. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which crash-test dummies in car safety testing shows Newton’s first and second laws.
items.answer: Cars are crashed at 64 km/h into barriers; sensors in dummies record the forces on the head and chest. The dummy keeps moving (first law) until a force stops it; airbags and crumple zones lengthen the stopping time, reducing deceleration and so the force (F = ma).
items.markingKey: Context (Cars are crashed at 64 km/h into barriers; sensors in dummies record the forces on the head and chest.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The dummy keeps moving (first law) until a force stops it; airbags and crumple zones lengthen the stopping time, reducing deceleration and so the force (F = ma). – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to Newton’s first and second laws.

items.stem: A student claims that a book on a table has no forces acting on it because it is not moving. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Weight and the normal contact force act on it; they are balanced.
items.markingKey: Weight and the normal contact force act on it; they are balanced. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which recoil of a fire hose shows interaction pairs.
items.answer: Firefighters must brace themselves because a high-pressure hose pushes back on them. The hose pushes water forwards; the water pushes the hose (and firefighter) backwards.
items.markingKey: Context (Firefighters must brace themselves because a high-pressure hose pushes back on them.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The hose pushes water forwards; the water pushes the hose (and firefighter) backwards. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to interaction pairs.

items.answer: Weight and air resistance still act; they are equal and opposite, so the resultant is zero.
items.markingKey: Weight and air resistance still act; they are equal and opposite, so the resultant is zero. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the introduction of compulsory seat belts in Victoria, Australia (1970, the world’s first) as an example, explain momentum and the forces in collisions.
items.answer: Road deaths in Victoria fell by around 18% in the following year. Belts stretch slightly, increasing the time to reduce the passenger’s momentum, reducing force; they also stop the passenger hitting the windscreen.
items.markingKey: Context (Road deaths in Victoria fell by around 18% in the following year.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Belts stretch slightly, increasing the time to reduce the passenger’s momentum, reducing force; they also stop the passenger hitting the windscreen. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to momentum and the forces in collisions.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that Newton’s third law means it is impossible to win a tug-of-war.
items.answer: The third law does not prevent winning; the winner pushes harder against the ground.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the rope tension pulls both teams equally. Arguments against: the team that pushes harder on the ground gets a larger forward friction force from the ground; the resultant force on each team depends on ground friction minus rope tension. Supported judgement: The third law does not prevent winning; the winner pushes harder against the ground. items.stem: Alessia investigated how the surface area of a paper parachute affects the time it takes to fall 2.0 m. The method had this weakness: the parachutes were thrown downwards rather than released. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: release each parachute from rest, already opened, at the same height
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: release each parachute from rest, already opened, at the same height

items.stem: "Lowering urban speed limits to 30 km/h is the best way to improve road safety." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It is one of the most effective measures, especially near schools, but works best combined with road design and enforcement.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: stopping distance much shorter, fewer collisions; pedestrian fatality risk falls sharply at lower impact speeds; less noise and pollution. Arguments against: longer journey times and possible driver frustration; enforcement is difficult; education, road design and vehicle safety also matter. Supported judgement: It is one of the most effective measures, especially near schools, but works best combined with road design and enforcement.
